--- title: "The Jackknife and Resampling Applications 🔪" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # The Jackknife and Resampling Applications

The jackknife: bias and standard error

Why it works, pseudovalues, and when it fails

Jackknife vs. bootstrap

Jackknife-after-bootstrap

Resampling for regression models and influence

::: notes - Rizzo 8.2 and Chapter 9, with material from A. I. McIntosh, "The Jackknife Estimation Method" (lecture notes, previously posted as Chapt8-Jackknife.pdf). ::: ## Resampling Methods: The Family - **Bootstrap** (Efron, 1979): resample $n$ points **with** replacement from the data; estimate the sampling distribution of $\hat\theta$. - **Permutation tests:** permute labels to obtain the null distribution of a test statistic (Rizzo Ch 10). - **Jackknife** (Quenouille, 1949; named by Tukey, 1956): leave out one observation at a time, i.e., resample **without** replacement, $n-1$ points. Originally for **bias correction**; Tukey added variance estimates and approximate confidence limits. ## Jackknife Samples and Replicates - The $i$th **delete-1 jackknife sample**: $x_{(i)} = (x_1,\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\dots,x_n)$; there are exactly $n$ of them. - The $i$th **jackknife replicate**: $\hat\theta_{(i)} = s(x_{(i)})$; their average $\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)} = \frac1n\sum_i\hat\theta_{(i)}$. ::: fact $$ \widehat\bias_{\text{jack}} = (n-1)\big(\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)} - \hat\theta\big),\qquad \widehat\se_{\text{jack}} = \sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\big(\hat\theta_{(i)} - \bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)}\big)^2}. $$ ::: - Deterministic: no random numbers, only $n$ recomputations. ## Why the Factor $(n-1)/n$? The Sample Mean For $\hat\theta = \bar x$: $\hat\theta_{(i)} = \dfrac{n\bar x - x_i}{n-1}$ and $\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)} = \bar x$, so $$ \hat\theta_{(i)} - \bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)} = \frac{\bar x - x_i}{n-1} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\big(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)}\big)^2 = \frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2 = \frac{S^2}{n}. $$ The jackknife SE of the mean is **exactly** the usual $S/\sqrt n$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); x <- rexp(12); n <- length(x) th.jack <- sapply(1:n, function(i) mean(x[-i])) c(jackknife = sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((th.jack - mean(th.jack))^2)), usual = sd(x) / sqrt(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` jackknife usual 0.1896 0.1896 ``` ::: ::: ## Why the Factor $(n-1)$ in the Bias? Suppose $\E[\hat\theta_n] = \theta + \dfrac{b_1(\theta)}{n} + \dfrac{b_2(\theta)}{n^2} + \cdots$. Each replicate uses $n-1$ points, so $$ \E\big[\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)}\big] - \E[\hat\theta] = \frac{b_1}{n-1} - \frac{b_1}{n} + O(n^{-3}) = \frac{b_1}{n(n-1)} + O(n^{-3}). $$ Multiplying by $(n-1)$ estimates the leading bias $b_1/n$. The **bias-corrected** estimator $$ \hat\theta_{\text{jack}} = \hat\theta - \widehat\bias_{\text{jack}} = n\hat\theta - (n-1)\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)} $$ has bias $O(n^{-2})$: the $1/n$ term cancels. **Check:** for $\hat\theta = \frac1n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$ (bias $-\sigma^2/n$), $\widehat\bias_{\text{jack}} = -S^2/n$ and $\hat\theta_{\text{jack}} = S^2$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pvar <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^2) th.jack <- sapply(1:n, function(i) pvar(x[-i])) c(bias_jack = (n - 1) * (mean(th.jack) - pvar(x)), minus_S2_over_n = -var(x) / n) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` bias_jack minus_S2_over_n -0.03593 -0.03593 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 8.6: Jackknife Bias of the Patch Ratio ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- nrow(patch); y <- patch$y; z <- patch$z theta.hat <- mean(y) / mean(z) theta.jack <- numeric(n) for (i in 1:n) theta.jack[i] <- mean(y[-i]) / mean(z[-i]) bias <- (n - 1) * (mean(theta.jack) - theta.hat) c(theta.hat = theta.hat, jackknife_bias = bias) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` theta.hat jackknife_bias -0.071306 0.008002 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 8.7: Jackknife SE of the Patch Ratio ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} se <- sqrt((n - 1) * mean((theta.jack - mean(theta.jack))^2)) c(jackknife_se = se) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` jackknife_se 0.1055 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) c(bootstrap_se = sd(boot(patch, function(d, i) mean(d$y[i]) / mean(d$z[i]), R = 2000)$t)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` bootstrap_se 0.103 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 8.8: Failure of the Jackknife The jackknife can fail when the statistic is **not smooth**. Median of 10 integers: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 10; set.seed(4750) x <- sample(1:100, size = n) M <- numeric(n) for (i in 1:n) M[i] <- median(x[-i]) Mbar <- mean(M) print(sort(M)) # only two distinct values! ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 47 47 47 47 47 49 49 49 49 49 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(jackknife_se = sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((M - Mbar)^2)), bootstrap_se = sd(replicate(1000, median(sample(x, replace = TRUE))))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` jackknife_se bootstrap_se 3.00 7.69 ``` ::: ::: ::: alert Fix for non-smooth statistics: the **delete-$d$ jackknife** with $\sqrt n < d < n-1$ (Shao and Wu, 1989): $\widehat\se_{d\text{-jack}} = \left\{\frac{n-d}{d\binom nd}\sum_z\big(\hat\theta_{(z)} - \bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)}\big)^2\right\}^{1/2}$. ::: ## Delete-$d$ Jackknife for the Median ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} djack_se <- function(x, d, stat = median, maxsub = 5000) { n <- length(x) subs <- if (choose(n, d) <= maxsub) combn(n, d) else replicate(maxsub, sample(n, d)) # all or a random subset th <- apply(subs, 2, function(z) stat(x[-z])) sqrt((n - d) / d * mean((th - mean(th))^2)) } set.seed(4750); x <- rnorm(40) c(delete1 = djack_se(x, 1), delete10 = djack_se(x, 10), bootstrap = sd(replicate(2000, median(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))), asymptotic = sqrt(pi / 2) / sqrt(40)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` delete1 delete10 bootstrap asymptotic 0.05027 0.26787 0.26189 0.19817 ``` ::: ::: ## Pseudovalues $$ \tilde\theta_i = n\hat\theta - (n-1)\hat\theta_{(i)},\qquad \hat\theta_{\text{jack}} = \frac1n\sum_i\tilde\theta_i,\qquad \widehat\se_{\text{jack}} = \frac{s_{\tilde\theta}}{\sqrt n}. $$ - Tukey: treat pseudovalues **as if** they were iid; a $t$-type interval $\hat\theta_{\text{jack}}\pm t_{n-1}\,\widehat\se_{\text{jack}}$. - Efron and Tibshirani: this interval is not much better than normal theory; prefer bootstrap intervals. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- nrow(patch); pseudo <- n * theta.hat - (n - 1) * theta.jack c(theta_jack = mean(pseudo), se = sd(pseudo) / sqrt(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` theta_jack se -0.07931 0.10553 ``` ::: ::: ## Example: Estimating the Upper Bound of a Uniform $X\sim U(0,\theta)$, $\hat\theta = X_{(n)}$ with $\E X_{(n)} = \frac{n}{n+1}\theta$ (biased). Here $\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)} = \frac{n-1}{n}X_{(n)} + \frac1nX_{(n-1)}$, so $$ \hat\theta_{\text{jack}} = X_{(n)} + \frac{n-1}{n}\big(X_{(n)} - X_{(n-1)}\big). $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); N <- 20000 res <- sapply(c(10, 30, 100), function(n) { r <- replicate(N, { s <- sort(runif(n, 0, 5)); mx <- s[n]; jk <- mx + (n - 1) / n * (mx - s[n - 1]) c(abs(5 - jk) < abs(5 - mx), abs(5 - jk), abs(5 - mx)) }) rowMeans(r) }) dimnames(res) <- list(c("P(|jack err| < |max err|)", "mean |jack - 5|", "mean |max - 5|"), c("n=10", "n=30", "n=100")) round(res, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n=10 n=30 n=100 P(|jack err| < |max err|) 0.6948 0.6762 0.6682 mean |jack - 5| 0.4343 0.1575 0.0498 mean |max - 5| 0.4588 0.1605 0.0503 ``` ::: ::: ::: notes - McIntosh's simulation: the jackknife estimate is closer about 68% of the time. Of course (n+1)/n * max is exactly unbiased here, but the jackknife does not need to know the distribution. ::: ## Jackknife vs. Bootstrap - Efron and Tibshirani: the jackknife variance estimate is $\frac{n}{n-1}$ times the **bootstrap variance of a linear approximation** $T_{\text{LIN}}(\mathbf P^*) = c_0 + (\mathbf P^* - \mathbf P_0)^\T\mathbf U$ to the statistic, where $\mathbf P^*$ is the vector of resampling proportions. - So the jackknife is excellent for **smooth (nearly linear)** statistics and poor for non-smooth ones (median, quantiles). - It assumes **iid** data: not for time series or correlated data without modification (block jackknife). | | Jackknife | Bootstrap | |---|---|---| | Resamples | $n$ deterministic | $B$ random | | Bias, SE | yes (smooth statistics) | yes | | Confidence intervals | rough | yes (percentile, BCa, $t$) | | Non-smooth statistics | fails (delete-1) | works | | Used for | BCa acceleration, influence, JaB | most inference | # Jackknife-after-Bootstrap (Rizzo 9.1) ## How Accurate Is $\widehat{\se}_B$? $\widehat\se_B(\hat\theta)$ is itself random. To estimate **its** standard error, leave out $x_i$, and recompute $\widehat\se_B$ using only the bootstrap samples that **do not contain** $x_i$: no new resampling! - $J(i)$ = indices of bootstrap samples not containing $x_i$; $B(i) = |J(i)|$. $$ \widehat\se_{B(i)} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{B(i)}\sum_{j\in J(i)}\big[\hat\theta^{(j)} - \bar{\hat\theta}_{(J(i))}\big]^2},\qquad \widehat\se\big(\widehat\se_B\big) = \widehat\se_{\text{jack}}\big(\widehat\se_{B(1)},\dots,\widehat\se_{B(n)}\big). $$ - On average $B(i)\approx B(1-1/n)^n\approx 0.37B$. ## Examples 9.1 - 9.2: JaB for the Patch Data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1111) theta.boot <- function(patch, i) mean(patch[i, "y"]) / mean(patch[i, "z"]) boot.out <- boot(patch, statistic = theta.boot, R = 2000) A <- boot.array(boot.out) # B x n matrix of frequencies theta.b <- boot.out$t n <- NROW(patch); jack.se <- numeric(n) for (i in 1:n) { keep <- which(A[, i] == 0) # samples that omit x_i jack.se[i] <- sd(theta.b[keep]) } c(se_boot = sd(theta.b), se_of_se = sqrt((n - 1) * mean((jack.se - mean(jack.se))^2)), avg_B_i = mean(colSums(A == 0))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` se_boot se_of_se avg_B_i 0.10098 0.02856 685.50000 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 9.11: The Jackknife-after-Bootstrap Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} jack.after.boot(boot.out, useJ = TRUE, stinf = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/15-jackknife/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - For each left-out observation: percentiles of $\hat\theta^* - \hat\theta$ (vertical) against the jackknife influence value (horizontal). Points far to the left/right are **influential**. # Resampling for Regression Models (Rizzo 9.2) ## Two Ways to Bootstrap a Regression :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Resampling cases** (pairs) - Resample rows $(x_i, y_i)$ with replacement; refit. - Robust to heteroscedasticity and model misspecification. - Treats $X$ as random. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Resampling errors** (residuals) - Fit; resample residuals $\hat e_j^*$; set $y_i^* = \hat y_i + \hat e^*_i$; refit. - Treats $X$ as fixed; assumes the model and iid errors. - Use **modified residuals** $r_i = \hat e_i/\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}$ (centered). ::: :::: ## Examples 9.5 - 9.6: Resampling Cases (Iron Data) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} L <- lm(magnetic ~ chemical, data = iron) m <- 2000; n <- NROW(iron); L1 <- numeric(m); set.seed(4750) for (b in 1:m) { i <- sample(1:n, replace = TRUE) L1[b] <- coef(lm(magnetic ~ chemical, data = iron[i, ]))[2] } beta_case <- function(dat, i) coef(lm(magnetic ~ chemical, data = dat[i, ]))[2] set.seed(4750); boot.cases <- boot(iron, beta_case, R = 2000) c(slope = coef(L)[2], se_lm = summary(L)$coef[2, 2], se_loop = sd(L1), se_boot = sd(boot.cases$t)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` slope.chemical se_lm se_loop se_boot 0.9158 0.1190 0.1219 0.1280 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} boot.ci(boot.cases, type = c("perc", "bca")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` BOOTSTRAP CONFIDENCE INTERVAL CALCULATIONS Based on 2000 bootstrap replicates CALL : boot.ci(boot.out = boot.cases, type = c("perc", "bca")) Intervals : Level Percentile BCa 95% ( 0.6662, 1.1590 ) ( 0.6885, 1.1947 ) Calculations and Intervals on Original Scale ``` ::: ::: ## Example 9.4: The `mammals` Data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mammals <- MASS::mammals par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(brain ~ body, data = mammals, pch = 16, main = "raw scale") plot(log(brain) ~ log(body), data = mammals, pch = 16, main = "log-log scale") L <- lm(log(brain) ~ log(body), data = mammals); abline(L, col = "red", lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/15-jackknife/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Examples 9.7 - 9.9: Resampling (Modified) Errors ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- log(mammals$brain); x <- log(mammals$body) L <- lm(y ~ x); n <- length(y) r <- residuals(L) / sqrt(1 - hatvalues(L)); r <- r - mean(r) # modified, centered residuals set.seed(4750); m <- 2000; estsE <- numeric(m) for (b in 1:m) { ystar <- fitted(L) + sample(r, replace = TRUE) estsE[b] <- coef(lm(ystar ~ x))[2] } model_based <- function(dat, i) { ystar <- dat$fit + dat$r[i]; coef(lm(ystar ~ dat$x))[2] } dat <- data.frame(x = x, fit = fitted(L), r = r) set.seed(4750); boot.err <- boot(dat, model_based, R = 2000) c(slope = coef(L)[2], se_lm = summary(L)$coef[2, 2], se_errors = sd(estsE), se_boot_fn = sd(boot.err$t)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` slope.x se_lm se_errors se_boot_fn 0.75169 0.02846 0.02868 0.02820 ``` ::: ::: ## Influence (Rizzo 9.3) - The **empirical influence value** of $x_i$ measures how much $\hat\theta$ changes when $x_i$ is up-weighted; the jackknife approximation is $l_{\text{jack},i} = (n-1)(\hat\theta - \hat\theta_{(i)})$. - $\sum_i l_i^2/n^2$ approximates $\var(\hat\theta)$ (the **nonparametric delta method**). **Example 9.10 (patch ratio):** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} L.inf <- empinf(boot.out, type = "jack") round(L.inf, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.0993 0.4004 -0.3489 0.4280 -0.1445 0.0892 -0.0451 -0.3438 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(se_delta = sqrt(sum(L.inf^2)) / n, se_boot = sd(boot.out$t)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` se_delta se_boot 0.01274 0.10098 ``` ::: ::: ## Summary ::: instructions - Jackknife: $n$ leave-one-out replicates; $\widehat\bias = (n-1)(\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta)$, $\widehat\se = \sqrt{\tfrac{n-1}{n}\sum(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)})^2}$. - Exact for the mean; removes $O(1/n)$ bias; fails for non-smooth statistics (use delete-$d$ or the bootstrap). - Jackknife-after-bootstrap: SE of bootstrap estimates and influence diagnostics with **no extra resampling**. - Regression: resample cases (robust) or errors (model-based, use modified residuals). :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
